title: lock, Interlocked, and synchronization primitives
hook: When multiple threads touch the same mutable state, you need synchronization. lock (Monitor) protects critical sections; Interlocked atomically updates integers; SemaphoreSlim limits concurrent access without blocking the entire object.

blocks.text: lock(obj) compiles to Monitor.Enter/Exit around a block — only one thread holds the lock at a time. Interlocked.Increment and CompareExchange perform atomic reads and writes without a full lock for simple counters. SemaphoreSlim allows N concurrent entrants — useful for throttling parallel HTTP calls. volatile is rarely needed in modern C# when you use proper synchronization or concurrent collections.

entries.plainDefinition: Language keyword that acquires a mutual-exclusion lock on an object.
Static methods for atomic operations on integers and references.
Lightweight semaphore limiting how many threads enter a region concurrently.

blocks.text: A shared in-memory counter for cache hits needs either Interlocked or lock. Never hold lock while awaiting Redis — you block other threads and can deadlock under load. Lock striping and concurrent collections reduce contention. Interviewers test whether you know the golden rule: protect in-memory state briefly; never lock across I/O.

blocks.title: Golden rule
blocks.body: Never hold a lock across await, HTTP, Redis, SQS, or database calls. Release the lock before I/O.

blocks.title: Synchronization
rows: Single-threaded event loop avoids most races
No lock keyword; mutex libs exist for workers

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Locking on this or typeof(MyType) — private readonly object is safer. await inside lock — compile error in modern C# but watch manual patterns. Locking a public string instance someone else might lock too.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: lock compiles to Monitor.Enter/Exit with a full memory barrier on release — subsequent reads see prior writes inside the critical section. volatile only guarantees ordered loads/stores for that field; it does not make check-then-act sequences atomic. Interlocked uses CPU atomic instructions with implicit barriers. Thread.VolatileWrite/Read and Interlocked.MemoryBarrier are explicit fences when you need publication without a full lock. Use dotnet-counters (ThreadPool ThreadCount, Lock Contention Rate) or a profiler to spot lock convoys under Redis cache miss storms.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Full barrier on exit; mutual exclusion
Counters, CompareExchange, lazy init of references
Prevents stale cached reads of one field
Shutdown/cancel flags; not for compound logic
No data visibility guarantee by itself
Throttle concurrent I/O; pair with proper shared-state rules

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying volatile makes any operation thread-safe — it only orders visibility for that field; _count++ still races. Claiming you need volatile inside every lock block — lock already publishes writes. Using volatile instead of Interlocked for metrics because it sounds lighter. Holding lock across await or Redis GET — blocks the pool and can deadlock under load.

interviewTakeaways: lock (Monitor) provides mutual exclusion and publishes writes on exit; Interlocked atomically updates single fields with implicit memory barriers.
volatile prevents stale reads of one flag but does not make check-then-act atomic — use Interlocked or lock for counters and invariants.
In production, watch ThreadPool queue length and lock contention counters when cache misses spike — convoys mean critical sections are too wide or held across I/O.

60s: lock for short multi-step invariants. Interlocked for counters. volatile only for simple publication of a boolean/int flag. Never await inside lock. SemaphoreSlim throttles parallel I/O, not data races.
Follow-up: when would you reach for Thread.MemoryBarrier instead of lock or Interlocked?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'volatile makes increment thread-safe' gets you rejected — volatile does not atomicize compound updates.
Lock across Redis or HTTP await — serializes the service and risks deadlock with the thread pool.
Strong answer: 'Monitor exit publishes writes. Interlocked for metrics. volatile for shutdown flags only. Profile lock contention with dotnet-counters before micro-optimizing.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: Node avoids many race conditions via one event loop. C# services are multi-threaded — shared state needs explicit synchronization.
Worker threads use Atomics.add for counters — the JS equivalent of Interlocked.Increment. There is no lock keyword; mutex libraries exist but are rare on the main thread.
